problem: Step 3 says the 200 ns scheduler decision 'is part of dispatch latency'. That contradicts the definition given two paragraphs earlier in Section 2 (dispatch latency = time to stop one process and start another, i.e. the dispatcher's work). It is fine to count the scheduler time in the switch overhead, but calling it part of dispatch latency will make students write the wrong definition in the exam.
fix: step 3: Scheduler cost: 200 ns — this is not dispatch latency, but it is CPU time lost on every switch, so it is counted in the total overhead.

problem: Section 1 says the figure traces the full life cycle, including admission 'from the job queue into the ready queue', but the figure has no job queue node and no admitted edge. A student comparing text and figure will look for a path that is not drawn.
fix: Add a 'Job queue' node with an 'admitted' edge to the ready queue (and update the aria text), or change the sentence to say the figure traces the paths after admission.

problem: The answer lumps two independent costs together. Register save/restore does scale with register count, but TLB size does not reliably make a switch dearer: a larger TLB can be invalidated by a single instruction or spared a flush entirely by address-space tags (ASIDs/PCIDs). Also, 'no cache of translations' on machine A cannot be read as 'cheaper', because without a TLB every access is slower. The qualifier 'tagged TLB entries' is attached to the register argument, where it does not belong.
fix: Answer along these lines: B must save and restore 64 registers instead of 8, so its register cost alone is about eight times A's; the TLB effect is separate — B pays more only if its entries must be invalidated on the switch, and pays nothing extra if they are tagged by address-space ID. The point stands that dispatch latency depends on register count, TLB design and memory speed, not on the OS alone.
